headline: Built self-destructing web tools on Cloudflare's free tier, solo for $0
summary: A developer created TempTools, a suite of free, no-signup web tools that automatically expire and delete data. It runs entirely on Cloudflare's free tier, showcasing robust serverless capabilities for solo projects.
details: Most cloud tools save data, but many tasks require temporary solutions. TempTools offers free, no-signup web tools like mock APIs, file sharing, and secret transfers that automatically expire and delete themselves. The entire suite was built solo on Cloudflare's free tier for $0.

The core challenge was ensuring exact expiry. Instead of relying solely on cron jobs, correctness is checked on the read path, meaning an item is deleted the moment it's accessed after expiry. Cron then acts as a janitor, sweeping up anything that expired but was never accessed.

For one-time secrets, the data is deleted immediately upon opening. For files, the associated R2 object is deleted after the response streams out, ensuring no lingering data. This dual-layer approach provides robust data removal.

During development, a challenge arose with Next.js 16's proxy (formerly middleware) defaulting to the Node.js runtime, which OpenNext on Cloudflare doesn't support for middleware. The fix involved dropping the proxy and handling redirects directly in next.config.ts.

To track basic usage without intrusive GDPR consent banners, the developer integrated Cloudflare Web Analytics. This cookieless and non-fingerprinting solution provides country-level traffic and basic numbers without requiring user consent.

Guardrails were implemented to manage free tier limits, especially for file storage. The application also supports ten languages with a [lang] segment, using hreflang and a sitemap for SEO, a strategy implemented from day one to avoid later retrofitting.

This project demonstrates the significant capabilities available to a single developer using a free serverless stack today. It highlights how a multi-tool app, with real storage, cron jobs, rate limiting, and analytics, can be run in multiple languages for no cost.

headline_marked: Index Ventures co-founder Neil Rimer says [[AI money will be redistributed]], voluntarily or involuntarily
headline: Index Ventures co-founder Neil Rimer says AI money will be redistributed, voluntarily or involuntarily
summary: A prominent venture capitalist believes the vast wealth generated by AI will undergo a significant redistribution. This comes as traditional philanthropy declines and legislative efforts for wealth taxes gain traction.
details: Index Ventures co-founder Neil Rimer predicts a "redistribution" of the wealth accumulating around AI, stating it will be "either voluntary or involuntary." He expressed this view at a tech festival in Athens, emphasizing tech leaders' role in this shift.

Rimer, who stepped back from day-to-day investing in 2021, co-founded one of the most successful venture firms of the last three decades. Index Ventures has raised approximately $15 billion and reportedly netted $9 billion from exits last year, including Figma and Wiz.

Despite his firm's success, Rimer has a history of personal philanthropy, serving on the board of Endeavor Greece and chairing Human Rights Watch. He also contributed $13 million to McGill University for an Indigenous Research and Knowledges institute.

His comments arrive as charitable giving trends show a decline. The Giving Pledge, launched by Buffett and Gates, has seen a significant drop in new signatories, with only four families joining in 2024.

Overall American charitable giving hit a record $592.5 billion in 2024, but the number of households donating has fallen for five consecutive years. Even affluent-household giving has slipped from 90% in 2017 to 81% last year.

This trend extends to Index's portfolio, including Anthropic. While Anthropic matches employee donations, a financial planner noted that most newly wealthy clients are focusing on angel investing or starting new companies rather than philanthropy.

The absence of voluntary giving is leading to legislative action, such as California's proposed 5% one-time wealth tax targeting billionaires. This has prompted some, like Google founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, to move their primary residences.

OpenAI is reportedly considering going public in 2027, potentially influenced by the California tax which would calculate net worth based on worldwide assets at the end of this year. Opposition to such wealth redistribution measures is significant, with concerns about wealthy residents relocating.
